batchName: Middle Republic: The Fall of Carthage and Corinth (167-133 BCE) - Hard Batch 1
chapterName: Middle Republic: The Fall of Carthage and Corinth (167-133 BCE)

questions.question: When a rash Roman attack on Hasdrubal's camp at Nepheris ended in heavy losses, what did Scipio Aemilianus do?
options: Covered the retreat with 300 cavalry and rescued trapped men at night
Burned the Carthaginian fleet in revenge
Took command from the consul and stormed the camp
Negotiated a truce with Hasdrubal
Abandoned the siege and returned to Rome
Rallied the Numidian allies to counter-attack
questions.explanation: Scipio, whose advice against the attack had been ignored, led 300 cavalry in disciplined charges and returned at night for trapped men. Visiting senators took note of his conduct.
questions.sourceQuote: Scipio led 300 cavalry in disciplined charges that covered the retreat, then rode back at night to rescue trapped men.

questions.question: In which year did Numantia finally fall, ending a struggle that had begun with its revolt in 154 BC?
options: 134 BC
146 BC
143 BC
133 BC
129 BC
151 BC
questions.explanation: Numantia fell in 133 BC, a year after Scipio took command in 134 BC. Afterwards Spain stayed largely at peace for more than half a century.
questions.sourceQuote: Numantia fell in 133 BC, and Spain stayed largely at peace for more than half a century.

questions.question: Which outcomes followed the fall of Carthage in 146 BC? (select all that apply)
options: Survivors were resettled 16 km inland
Hasdrubal was killed in the Temple of Eshmoun
About 50,000 survivors were sold into slavery
Sacred statues were returned to Sicilian cities
The Romans sowed the ground with salt
The Roman deserters were pardoned
questions.explanation: Around 50,000 survivors were enslaved, and statues Carthage had looted from Sicilian cities were ceremonially returned. The salting story is probably a 19th-century invention.
questions.sourceQuote: Around 50,000 survivors were sold into slavery.

questions.question: How did the Carthaginians respond to Scipio's harbour mole in 147 BC?
options: They wrecked it with fireships
They dug a secret channel and sailed out a new fleet
They tunnelled under the city walls
They bribed the Roman engineers
They surrendered the harbour district
They called the Macedonian fleet to break it
questions.explanation: Carthage secretly dug a new channel to the sea and sailed out with a newly built fleet. They held their own, but many ships were trapped against the sea wall and lost as they withdrew.
questions.sourceQuote: The Carthaginians secretly dug a new channel to the sea and sailed out with a newly built fleet.

questions.question: Why did the Roman plan of 123 BC to found a new colony on the site of Carthage collapse?
options: Plague broke out among the colonists
Numidian raids destroyed the settlers
The Senate's ten-man commission blocked it
Utica refused to provide a harbour
Rumours that wolves dug up its boundary markers
The first emperor vetoed it
questions.explanation: Opponents spread rumours that wolves had dug up the colony's boundary markers, a terrible omen, and the plan collapsed. A new Roman Carthage was only completed in 29 BC by the man who became Rome's first emperor.
questions.sourceQuote: Opponents spread rumours that wolves had dug up its boundary markers, a terrible omen, and the plan collapsed.

questions.question: Who wrote the one complete ancient narrative of the Third Punic War, and when?
options: It survives only on coins and inscriptions
It was written by Cato as propaganda
It was Polybius's draft, later heavily edited
It was written three centuries later by a Greek author
It was written by a Carthaginian exile
It survives only as a list of contents
questions.explanation: The only complete narrative was written by a Greek author in the 2nd century AD, three centuries after the war. It seems to draw mainly on Polybius, but scholars have found several problems with it.
questions.sourceQuote: The one complete narrative of the war was written by a Greek author in the 2nd century AD, three centuries later.

questions.question: What happened to the general Hasdrubal after the disaster at Oroscopa in 151 BC?
options: He died on the battlefield
He escaped home and was condemned to death by Carthage
He was hailed a hero and made ruler
He was handed to Rome as a hostage
He was executed by the Numidians
He fled into exile at Utica
questions.explanation: Carthage condemned Hasdrubal to death in a bid to placate Rome, but it was too late. He was later released to lead a field army when Rome attacked.
questions.sourceQuote: Hasdrubal escaped home, where his own city condemned him to death in a bid to placate Rome.

questions.question: What did the Roman embassy of 147 BC announce to the Achaean League, sparking war?
options: It must join Rome's war on Carthage
It must return its hostages to Rome
It must hand over Corinth's fleet
It must dissolve entirely
It must pay a heavy indemnity
It must shrink back to its original core
questions.explanation: The embassy demanded the League shrink back to its original core, and the envoys were nearly mobbed. War followed, ending with Mummius routing the Greeks outside Corinth.
questions.sourceQuote: The next year a Roman embassy announced that the League must shrink back to its original core; the envoys were nearly mobbed.

questions.question: Which measures did Carthage take after rejecting Rome's ultimatum in 149 BC? (select all that apply)
options: Hired Celtiberian mercenaries
Handed Utica to the Numidians
Moved its population 16 km inland
Released Hasdrubal to lead a field army
Recalled its warships from Utica
Freed slaves willing to fight
questions.explanation: Carthage freed slaves who were willing to fight and released the condemned general Hasdrubal to lead a field army. Its huge walls, with barracks for 24,000 soldiers built inside, also gave it a strong defence.
questions.sourceQuote: Slaves willing to fight were freed, and Hasdrubal, the general recently condemned to death, was released to lead a field army.

questions.question: What do historians say about the origin of the famous phrase 'Carthage must be destroyed' (Carthago delenda est)?
options: It was inscribed on Cato's tomb
It survives in Livy's surviving books
It is a later tradition credited to Cato since the 18th century
Scipio coined it at Numantia
Polybius recorded Cato saying it
Cato's speeches show it word for word
questions.explanation: Cato has been credited with ending every speech with the phrase only since the 18th century. It is a later tradition rather than a quotation recorded by ancient writers.
questions.sourceQuote: The phrase is a later tradition rather than a quotation recorded by ancient writers.
